name: Fine-Tuning and LoRA
intent: Understand what it costs to train a model further, and how low-rank adapters let a team change a model's behaviour by training a tiny fraction of its weights.
scenario: A support team wants a 7-billion-parameter model to answer in the company's tone. They have one GPU with 24 GB of memory, and full fine-tuning of the model would not fit on it.
problem: Training does not only need the weights. For every weight being trained, the optimizer also keeps its gradient and extra running statistics. With the usual mixed-precision Adam setup that is about 16 bytes for each trainable parameter, so a 7-billion-parameter model needs around 112 GB of training state before any activations are stored. Most teams cannot afford that, and many do not need to change every weight to change a behaviour.

howItWorks.title: Full fine-tuning trains every weight
howItWorks.text: Each weight is updated, so each needs a gradient and optimizer state. In the ZeRO paper's accounting for mixed-precision Adam this comes to about 16 bytes per parameter: 2 for the 16-bit weight, 2 for its gradient and 12 for the 32-bit optimizer states. The result is a full new copy of the model for every task.

howItWorks.title: LoRA freezes the weights and adds a small update
howItWorks.text: Low-rank adaptation keeps each original weight matrix W frozen and learns a small update next to it. The update is the product of two thin matrices, B (d x r) and A (r x d), where the rank r is small, such as 8. The layer computes with W plus B x A.

howItWorks.title: Count the trainable weights
howItWorks.text: A matrix of size d x d has d x d weights. Its LoRA update has d x r + r x d = 2 x d x r. For d = 4096 and r = 8 that is 65536 instead of 16777216, about 0.391 percent. Only these small matrices need gradients and optimizer state.

howItWorks.title: Start from the original model
howItWorks.text: B starts at zero, so the model begins exactly as the base model did, and training moves it away from there. After training, B x A can be added into W, so the tuned model runs with no extra delay. The LoRA paper reported 10,000 times fewer trainable parameters and 3 times lower hardware needs than full fine-tuning of GPT-3 175B, with quality on par or better in their tests.

howItWorks.title: Adapters are small and swappable
howItWorks.text: The result of training is a small file of adapter weights. One shared base model can serve many tasks or customers by loading a different adapter for each, instead of storing a full copy of the model for every one.

howItWorks.title: QLoRA shrinks the base model too
howItWorks.text: QLoRA keeps the frozen base model in 4-bit form and trains LoRA adapters through it. The QLoRA paper reported fine-tuning a 65-billion-parameter model on a single 48 GB GPU, where regular 16-bit fine-tuning needs more than 780 GB. Data quality, evaluation and avoiding forgetting matter as much as the method.

pros: Training state is a tiny fraction of full fine-tuning, so one GPU can be enough
Adapter files are small, so one base model can serve many tasks
Adapters can be merged into the weights, with no extra inference latency
A bad run is cheap to throw away, because the base model is untouched
cons: A low-rank update may not capture every change that full fine-tuning could
The frozen base model still has to be loaded in memory, at 16-bit or 4-bit size
Choosing the rank, the layers to adapt and the learning rate takes experiments
It changes behaviour, but does not reliably add facts or fix a base model's weaknesses
whenToUse: You need a consistent style, format or skill and have good examples
Full fine-tuning does not fit in your GPU memory or budget
You serve several tasks or customers from one base model
whenNotToUse: Do not use fine-tuning to teach facts that change: retrieval keeps them current
Do not fine-tune before trying prompting and examples, and before you have an evaluation set
Do not fine-tune on a small, narrow set without checking that general ability has not dropped
pitfalls: Training on examples with errors or inconsistent style, so the model learns the noise
Evaluating only on the tuning topics and missing a loss of general ability
Forgetting that a new base model version needs the adapters to be trained again
Counting only the trainable parameters when sizing memory, and not the frozen base model

quiz.question: A team wants to adapt a 7-billion-parameter model on one 24 GB GPU. Full fine-tuning needs about 16 bytes per parameter, roughly 112 GB, for training state alone. What is the best approach?
options: Train on a smaller sample of the data, which reduces the memory needed for every weight
Lower the learning rate, because a smaller step needs less optimizer memory per weight
Use LoRA, perhaps with a 4-bit base model, so that only small adapter matrices need training state
Fine-tune only the last layer in full precision, and leave the model's other weights unchanged
quiz.explanation: Training state is proportional to the number of trainable weights. LoRA trains a tiny fraction of them, and a 4-bit base (QLoRA) shrinks the frozen part as well. The amount of data and the learning rate do not change the memory per weight, and a single full-precision layer is a different, usually weaker, method.

quiz.question: A software company wants a different tone and vocabulary for each of 200 customers, from one shared base model. Why do LoRA adapters fit this well?
options: Each adapter is a small file, so one base model can be loaded once and a different adapter used for each customer
Adapters make the base model larger, so that it can store the facts of each customer
Adapters remove the need for any evaluation, because they cannot change the model's behaviour
Each customer's adapter must be merged into one file, so that all customers share the same tone
quiz.explanation: The adapter is tiny compared with the base model, so many can be stored and swapped on top of a single copy of it. Adapters do not enlarge the base model, they still need evaluation, and merging them into one file would remove the separation between customers.

quiz.question: After LoRA fine-tuning at rank 8, answers on the company's topics improve, but the model is worse at general questions it used to handle well. What is the most likely cause?
options: The rank is too low, so the model cannot learn anything and returns to its old behaviour
The narrow training data pulled the model towards it, so mix in general examples, tune gently and evaluate broadly
The base model was damaged, because LoRA overwrites the original weights permanently
The adapter is too small to matter, so the general degradation must come from the hardware
quiz.explanation: Training on a narrow set can shift behaviour on everything, and the loss of general ability needs to be measured and managed with broader data and gentler settings. The base weights are frozen, so they are not overwritten, and the hardware is not to blame.
